transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Uh, yeah… I guess I’m here because the doctor who did my insurance physical said my weight was too low. I mean, I don’t really see it that way—I’m a painter, so I’m up and down ladders all day, carrying stuff, long days, you know. Kind of just figured I’m lean from work. My uncle was the same way, actually, always wiry from doing construction… but yeah, the insurance doctor seemed concerned, so here I am.
Have you noticed any unintentional weight loss or changes in your appetite lately?

I mean, I wouldn’t call it unintentional exactly… I just don’t really eat much during the day. Most days it’s coffee, maybe a protein bar if I’m between jobs or stopped at a gas station, and then a small dinner later. A big lunch just makes me feel kind of heavy, like it slows me down, especially when I’m up on a ladder or cutting in trim. One time I had a burrito before doing ceilings and I swear I felt useless all afternoon, so I kind of learned not to do that.
Do you ever skip meals or eat less than you think you should because you're worried about gaining weight or because of how you perceive your body?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t sit there thinking, like, “I can never gain weight” all day or anything. But if I go to a client dinner or have, you know, bread or pasta or something heavier, and then the scale is up even a little the next morning, I get… tense, I guess. Like it bothers me more than it probably should.

So then I’ll usually cut back the next day—skip more, keep it lighter—just so it doesn’t stick. I had this one client who always wanted to order Italian after a job, really nice guy, talked forever about restoring old houses, and I’d be sitting there thinking about how much bread was on the table instead of the conversation. So… yeah, I guess that happens.
After eating more than usual or having something heavier, do you ever do extra physical activity or anything else specifically to try to burn off the calories or keep your weight down?

I don’t know… not like a plan, exactly. My work is physical anyway, so it’s hard to separate. If I had a heavier dinner, the next day I might be more… aware of it, I guess, but I’m not going out jogging at midnight or anything.

Sometimes I’ll take on the more active parts of a job, like moving drop cloths or doing ladder work, but that’s also just the job. Painting sounds simple but people don’t realize how much carrying and prep there is—half the time you’re sanding or taping forever before any paint even goes on. So… I’m not sure if that counts as doing extra to burn it off.
Do you find yourself going out of your way to avoid gaining any weight, even if it means feeling hungry or not eating enough?

Yeah… I guess I do. Not in some dramatic way, but if the scale bumps up even a little after, like, a client dinner or something with bread, I get really tense about it. Then the next day I’ll kind of rein it in—eat lighter, skip more—just so it doesn’t, I don’t know, stick.

It’s stupid because sometimes those dinners are just part of the job, like people want to be nice after you finish painting their place, and you’re sitting there nodding about their kitchen cabinets or whatever, but in my head I’m already thinking about what the scale’s gonna say. So… yeah, I’ll put up with being hungry if it means keeping it from going up.
Do you see yourself as underweight, normal weight, overweight, or obese—even when others might tell you otherwise?

I guess… I’d probably say normal, technically, but I don’t really feel it that way. Like if I catch myself in a mirror, or in a photo next to one of my murals or a finished wall, I’ll zoom in on whether my face looks too full or if my stomach looks flat enough.

It’s weird, because the mural could’ve taken me days, and instead of looking at the work I’m like, “Do I look sharp enough there?” And then that kind of decides how I feel about the whole day, which sounds ridiculous saying it out loud.
Have you ever made yourself vomit, taken laxatives, or done anything else to try to get rid of food after eating more than you meant to?

Um… I don’t really know. I mean, I’ve felt gross after eating too much, like that too-full feeling, and then I get kind of stuck thinking about it. But making myself throw up or taking something… I’m not sure how to answer because I don’t really—like, I’m usually more in my head about what I ate than doing some specific thing after.

I’ve had jobs where I’m up and down ladders all day and my stomach feels off anyway, especially if I ate something heavy before painting in a hot room, and then you’re smelling primer for hours, which doesn’t help. But that’s not really what you’re asking, I guess.

So… I don’t have a clear “yes” to that. I mostly just get uncomfortable and try to move past it.
Have you ever fasted for a full day, used diet pills, or done anything else specifically to prevent weight gain after eating more than you meant to?

I don’t use diet pills or anything like that. Fasting for a whole day… not really in some planned, official way. It’s more like if I had a client dinner, especially with bread or a heavier meal, and then the scale is up even a little the next morning, I get really tense.

Then I’ll start cutting back the next day—eat lighter, maybe skip more than I normally would—just to make sure it doesn’t stick. It’s hard to explain, because part of me knows it could just be, I don’t know, salt or whatever, but once I see the number, it kind of gets in my head. Then I’m thinking about it while I’m working, like rolling paint on a wall and still doing the math in my head.
Would you say that your overall sense of self-worth or how you feel about yourself is strongly influenced by your body weight or shape?

Yeah… I think it is, more than I’d like to admit. Like, I can have a good workday, finish a mural that a client is happy with, and then if I see a photo of myself beside it and my face looks too round or my stomach doesn’t look flat enough, it kind of ruins it for me.

I’ll be standing there supposed to be proud of the wall, or thinking about the colors or the lines, and instead I’m judging whether I look “sharp” enough. And then that ends up deciding how I feel about myself that day, which… yeah, I guess that means it has a pretty strong effect.
Has your concern about your weight or shape ever gotten in the way of your work, relationships, or other important parts of your life?

Yeah… a little, I guess. I still get my jobs done. Like, I’m not missing painting work or leaving walls half-finished or anything. Once I’m on-site I can usually just focus on the prep and the lines and getting the coat even.

But it gets in the way more around the edges. I’ll avoid client lunches or dinners sometimes, especially if it’s one of those “come eat with us after” things, because then it becomes this whole situation in my head. People might notice what I order, or say something like “you’re not eating much,” or comment on how I look. Even if they mean nothing by it, I’ll think about it for the rest of the day.

And social plans too. I’ve backed out of stuff if I think food’s going to be a big part of it. Not always, but enough that… yeah, it does get in the way.
Do you restrict your food intake most days because of fears about gaining weight or because of how you perceive your body shape?

Yeah… most days, probably. I don’t always think of it as “restricting,” because it just feels like how I keep the day moving, you know?

Like if I’m working, I’ll usually just have coffee, maybe a protein bar between jobs if I’m starting to feel shaky or if I know I’ve got a ladder setup or something. Then I’ll do a small dinner later. A full meal during the day feels like it would slow me down, or sit in my stomach, and then I start thinking about how I look in my work clothes, which is stupid because they’re covered in paint half the time anyway.

But yeah… it is tied to not wanting to gain weight. I guess I kind of build the day around keeping things light.
Do you find that your thoughts about your body weight or shape dominate your thinking, even when you're trying to focus on other things?

Yeah… it can, even when I’m trying not to let it. Like I’ll be painting, trying to think about the spacing or whether the color is drying right, and then I catch myself in a window reflection or someone takes a photo of me next to the mural, and suddenly that’s all I’m looking at.

Not the work, not whether the client likes it—just whether my stomach looks flat enough or my face looks sharp enough. And then somehow that decides if the whole day feels okay or ruined. I know that sounds… kind of ridiculous, but it really does take over in those moments.
Have you ever done anything like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising far more than usual specifically to prevent weight gain, even if it was just occasionally?

Um… I don’t know. I mean, I’ve thought about that kind of thing in a general way, like you hear people talk about it or see it in movies, but I don’t really… I’m not sure I’d say that’s been my thing.

Exercise is tricky because my work is physical anyway—up ladders, sanding, hauling paint, all that—so sometimes I’m exhausted by the end of the day without trying. Like last week I was doing this exterior job and the wind kept blowing dust into the primer, and I swear I went up and down the ladder a hundred times, but that wasn’t like… planned for weight or anything.

So, yeah, I don’t think I have a clear answer beyond… not really that I’ve noticed.
Would you say that your body weight or shape has a significant impact on how you feel about yourself overall?

Yeah… I think it does, more than I like admitting.

It’s not like I wake up and say, “My whole worth depends on this,” but then I’ll catch myself in a mirror or see a photo of me standing next to one of my murals, and instead of looking at the work—like the lines, the colors, whether the wall came out right—I’m zooming in on my stomach or my face.

If my stomach looks flat enough or my face looks kind of sharp, then I feel like, okay, I’m doing alright. And if not, it can kind of sour the whole day. Which is dumb, because the mural might be good, the client might be happy, but I’m still stuck on how I looked in the picture.
